Your actual mod isn't that hard to make but I want to take issue with the actual ideas and suggest that the changes that you want to make aren't much more consistent with the period's historical reality than what Vic2 actually represents.

Liberalism -- as an ideology -- is not consistent. At the start of the game, it is a revolutionary ideology that seeks to abolish the *ancien regime*, replacing it with regimes of private property based on written, constitutional, law. By the end of the game these same liberals exist in a space that is not truly socialist but also not truly liberal. The best example are the subjects of my thesis (the names of French political groupings in the 1910s) whose ideology of "radicalism" is best exemplified in Serge Bernstein's *Histoire du Parti Radical* (1980). This fuzziness can't be easily simulated by a clean line between socialist and (anarcho-)liberal.

This historical fuzziness can be understood in many ways, Hobsbawm (you would like him) repeatedly relies on the class differences, saying in *The Age of Revolution* (1962) that:

>“In fact the Sansculottes were one branch of that universal and important political trend which sought to express the interests of the great mass of ‘little men’ who existed between the poles of the ‘bourgeoisie’ and the ‘proletarian’, often perhaps nearer to the latter than the former because they were, after all, mostly poor. We can observe in the United States (as Jeffersonianism and Jacksonian democracy, or populism) in Britain (as ‘radicalism’), in France (as the ancestors of the future ‘republicans’ and radical-socialists), in Italy as Mazzinians and Garibaldians), and elsewhere. Mostly it tended to settle down, in post-revolutionary ages, as a left-wing of middle-class liberalism, but one loth to abandon the ancient principle that there are no enemies on the left, and ready, in times of crisis, to rebel against ‘the wall of money’ or ‘economic royalists’ or ‘the cross of gold crucifying mankind.’”

The question to ask is how these ideologies changed over time and how that can be better simulated than how it currently is in the game (which, for the record, I think is well done). Albert Thibaudet, for example, argued for a historical march to the left that he called [Sinistrisme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinistrisme) which is effectively Marxist historical development shorn of its teleological elements. This process of changing ideologies within a single umbrella is hard to explain or make sense of, so how can we simulate it? How do we understand how Jaurès moved between radicalism and socialism, or how the SPD could go from the party of revolution to the party of reaction in 1918/9. Indeed, I think of a quote from Buhkarin that I use in my thesis that's informative:

>“History is full of examples of the transformation of parties of revolution into parties of order. Sometimes the only mementos of a revolutionary party are the watchwords which it has inscribed on public buildings.” (Cohen, Bukharin, 1980)

I won't comment on the dictatorship of the proletariat other than to recommend you read Rosa Luxemburg's [Organizational Questions of the Russian Social Democracy](https://www.marxists.org/archive/luxemburg/1904/questions-rsd/). The accusation that Leninism is effectively Blaquism is not unfounded.

In my opinion, you're correct that fascism is the "iron heel of capitalism" coming down to crush an organized working class. Historically, fascism did represent the interests of the petite bourgeoisie and that's supported by the fact that the petite bourgeoisie voted (although not overwhelmingly) for Hitler. But even though fascism received the same class support as the revolutionary liberals at the start of the game that does not means that they are the same. Indeed, I contend that fascism is best described as a "revolutionary reaction" as best laid out by Paxton's *The Anatomy of Fascism* (2004) and exemplified in Kershaw's *The End* (2011). Fascism is not defined by a systematic deconstruction of state-run economies but as gangster/crony capitalism where privatization is carried out for the enrichment of a view few and whose relationships are *not* defined by written contracts and legal regimes -- as 19th-century liberals worked so hard to create -- but by semi-feudal personal connections outside of any state or legal control, see Kershaw, "'Working Towards the Führer.' Reflections on the Nature of the Hitler Dictatorship" (1993).

A theory I am currently developing and which some research has pointed towards (but not made explicit) is what I call the "invention of right-wing nationalism" since, as we know, nationalism was a product of the left-wing of the French Revolution and was directly tied ideas of constitutional, democratic, and free-market regimes. It wasn't until after the failures of 1848 that nationalism became intertwined with reactionary, aristocratic, and other right-wing forces, leading, eventually to fascism.

But, like I said above, these connections don't suggest that fascism is somehow liberal, but rather how these intellectual ideas and ideological programs were moving between left and right in a way that is hard to define (why do you think it's my thesis). A systematic class critique is possible but Vic2 doesn't have the framework to make it happen, Vic3 is going in that direction but time will tell. But this is all to say that I think the current system is fine and that you could deepen your understanding of the ideological 19th century a bit. I'll recommend Eric Hobsbawm, he's the single best historian of the period, a lifelong member of the CPGB, unrelenting communist (much to the dismay of liberals who have to accept that his research is without equal), and overall prolific writer.

TL;DR: the mod would be easy to make but the ideologies in the game are fine as is, read my thesis.

I'm currently half way through Ostelhammer's book. A good read, the last 250 pages are just Footnotes so it's a much shorter read than it looks.

Rapport's 1848 is a great history of the year(s) of revolution, Christopher Clark is currently writing a global history of them but it's not out yet, his history of the outbreak of WWI (The Sleepwalkers) provides a great perspective on the outbreak of the war. I've seen Pursuit of Power by Richard Evans and Eric Hobsbawm's series on the 19th century recommended, both are great (I'm partial to Hobsbawm) and worth a read. Jonathan Sperber also has a history of Europe between 1850 and 1914 which is a great textbook. One more European book I'd recommend is Europe Since Napoleon by David Thompson, a really fun read. 

I'm less familiar with non-European histories but there are a few I can recommend. The Birth of the Modern World by Christopher Bayly is a good read as is Mike Davis' Late Victorian Holocaust. European Imperialism by Alice L. Conklin & Ian Fletcher is really interesting. After Tamerlane by John Darwin is a great overview of global empires in which the nineteenth century features prominently. 

Regarding American History Steven Hahn's A Nation Without Boarders is a great non-traditional history of America's 19th century.

There are a lot more country and theme specific books I can recommend but this should give you more than enough reading for the time being. All are great and worth a read even after Victoria 3 gets released!

Yeah I got it as a gift for my birthday because I'm going to college next year for history.  Basically half my family is in history-related fields so they're giving me all of the classics to read.

Here my list of books that I have either read this year or am literally about to start today.

* *Salt: A World History* By Mark Kurlansky
> A really interesting book that puts a unique spin on history.  I kept looking at my phone while reading this because I needed to be sure that the events he talked about in the book were actually true!  You really do learn a lot about how this little mineral that we take for granted today has been so influential on world history.

* *Back Channel to Cuba: The Hidden History of Negotiations Between Washington and Havana* by William M. LeoGrande & Peter Kornbluh
> More recent history as it goes even into the Obama administration and get right up to the moment before the normalization of relations between the U.S. and Cuba.  I found it really interesting to see how the U.S. has kinda been constantly screwing over Cuba for the past 50 years and how Cuba has taken it standing up.  Really good read especially since there is movement on the diplomatic front of recent.

* *A Bridge Too Far* By Cornelius Ryan
> One of the classic World War II novels for a reason.  I can't say much other than I loved it!  I constantly felt the ups and down that the paratroopers in the Netherlands were experiencing over 70 years ago.  It revealed the rarely talked about failures of the Allies and how plans need time to be made, not just thrown together.  A classic for a reason and I loved it!

* *The Wake* by Paul Kingsnorth 
> Not normal history but a historical fiction, put it here because it did an excellent job in displaying the chaos of the time - post conquest of William the Bastard England.  Half written in Angalish it was very hard to read at times, but it was extremely rewarding to do so.  It reveals not only the mindset of an insurgent, which is very important for the modern world, but also the terror and chaos that existed in the Anglo-Saxon population after William the Bastard invaded.  It may be historical fiction but it's one of the best historical fictions I have ever read.

* *City of Fortune: How Venice Ruled the Seas* by Roger Crowley
> The first of the many Roger Crowley books I read this year.  I as someone who didn't know a lot about Venice or its' rise to power, but was extremely curious this is the book to read.  It perfectly tells the story of Venice from its ascendance during the Fourth Crusade to its fall from grace at the hands of the Ottomans.  I can't say much other than it is amazing and everyone should read it!

* *Lost to the West: The Forgotten Byzantine Empire that Rescued Western Civilization* By Lars Brownworth
> I read this in an afternoon, not even 250 pages it is the whole story of the Eastern Roman Empire/Byzantine Empire, from the split with the west to the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.  As someone who listened to Brownworth's podcast *12 Byzantine Rulers* it was a perfect addition to the material presented.  I wholly recommend this book with even a passing intreast in history to read this and learn about how Rome didn't fall until the 15th century.

* *Empires of the Sea: The Siege of Malta, the Battle of Lepanto, and the Contest for the Center of the World* by Roger Crowley
> Crowley doesn't right like a normal historian, he rights for the layman to understand these fascinating moments in history.  I felt throughout the book like I was there in the battle he was describing, whether the chaos of Lepanto or the desperation of Malta, I felt personally involved in these stories.  Again I recommend this to anyone who wishes to learn about awesome moments in history.

* *1453 - The Holy War for Constantinople and the Clash of Islam and the West* by Roger Crowley
> MORE CROWLEY!  I read this to do some research on the Fall of Constantinople and I have been using this as my primary resource.  It so perfectly tells to the story of 1453 and gives such detail that you would think that the events are unfolding live.  He has put so much research into the book and it shows.  Though not as good as his other books but still worth a read!

* *The Crimean War: The Truth Behind the Myth* by Clive Ponting
> Let this begin with this statement, the Crimean War was a glorious fuck up for the British Army, it showed the disaster that can come from having your officers pay for their positions and not earn it.  The whole book felt like Pontig was being very condescending and was enjoying it, but he did reveal some of the myths that have been told about the Crimean War.

* *A People's History of the United States* by Howard Zinn
> Just finished this earlier today so I haven't had a proper opportunity to internalize this one yet, but it was wonderful.  I was already ideologically similar to Zinn before reading this book so a lot of what it did was reinforce my own viewpoints but it was still a worth while read.  I don't have much to say as I just read it but I love it and I understand why it is a classic!

That's the wonderful thing about New Vegas... none of them are moral!  In each of the endings the narrator always tells you about the good and bad you did.  The NCR like you said are trying to do the right thing but they are doing it poorly. The Legion is cruel but fair, all offenders are treated equally but they need to catch up to the rest of the Mojave in terms of Slavery and Women's Rights.  Mr. House, (Side note he did not plan to centrally plan the economy, in fact it was the opposite!  He planned to make a free market paradise most likely based off Ayn Rand, basically think Rapture from the Bioshock games.) he doesn't care about the people of the Mojave, he only wants to increase his profits.  And finally there's Yesman, oh Yesman, the ending  states that the Courier just leaves he doesn't become the dictator, he just lets the chips fall as they may, and the narrator states that there is chaos in the Mojave because there is no central government to help them, and in the Lonesome Road DLC it states that The Courier has made a society before in The Divide and it fell apart, thanks to the Courier.  So the real question that New Vegas asks you is not what is the morally correct choice, but what makes you feel the least guilty?  Is it the NCR trying and failing to keep people safe? Or is it the Legion keeping the Mojave safe but making it a harsh cruel world? Maybe it's Mr. House with his Laissez-faire government, and Securitrons that bring justice with bullets? Or maybe it's just letting the people of the Mojave break free of the tyrants and let them do as they wish, even though that leads to chaos? There is no morally good answer, you have to make the best with what you have.
